First, lets install some packages we will use today: 

## Installing packages

```{r, eval=FALSE}

install.packages("data.table")
install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("forcats")
install.packages("reshape2")

```

If you are questioned if you want to install the packages from source or update other packages, you can accept. If you face problems, try again answering `no`. 

### The libPaths problem: 

Optional, if the package installation doesn't work: If you get error messages that describe that you can't install the packages, the problem is likely that R has no writing access in the directory of your package library. 

```{r}
.libPaths() # This shows you the currently used directory (the first entry):
```

To solve the problem, we generate and use another directory for our libraries: 

```{r, eval = FALSE}
user_lib <- Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER") # find personal standard library directory
dir.create(user_lib, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) # Create directory
.libPaths(c(user_lib, .libPaths())) # Activate it
.libPaths() # check if it worked
```

The `.libPaths()` call should show the new directory as first entry. Restart `RStudio` and try to install the package again, using the `install.packages()` line above. If that doesn't work, restart `RStudio`with administrator rights and try again. 

## Load packages: 

```{r}
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

```




## Import data:

Lets explore our DepMap cell line model/patient data. First, we import it using `fread()` and assign it to the variable `models`: 

```{r, eval = FALSE}
models <- fread("input_data/Model.csv")
```

Importing and cleaning data can be complicated, and I want to make sure that everybody is working with the same data. Please execute this script, which loads packages and required input data. You can always re-load the script if you accidently replaced it.  

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
source("R/prepare_everything.R")
```

## Handling Datatables

`data.table` is a modern R package which introduces a compact syntax and very fast data handling. This is perfect for operations on the datasets we want to work with today. 
`Data.tables` are enhanced `data.frames`, which makes them compatible with the `tidyverse` functions as well as `ggplot2`. 
Datatables/dataframes are perfect for storing different datatypes for many observations, e.g. age (numeric), sex (categorical), treatment status (logical), etc., across patients. Datatables are in most cases two-dimensional, with observations / measurements / patients in rows and features in columns. 

The data table syntax consists of three elements: 

`DT[<rows>, <columns>, <by>]`. 

`<rows>` defines the rows to extract from the `DT`. Often used with filter criteria. 
`<columns>` defines the columns to select. Can also be used to create new columns or to execute functions in the data table. 
`by` defines variables to group the data by. Can be used to elegantly summarize the information of the datatable. 

Examples: 

```{r}
str(models)
```

```{r}
head(models)
```


To only select certain columns, we wrap them in `.()`.  This is usually done **after** the first comma: 

```{r}
models[, .(Sex, Age)]
```

Important data.table operator: `.N` returns the number of rows.  

```{r}
models[, .N]
```

`.N` is particularly useful when combined with a grouping variable after the second comma. We can write `by = `, but we don't have to. 
Lets explore how many male and female patients (and patients with unknown sex) are in the dataset: 

```{r}
models[, .N, by = Sex]
```

This gives you a good overview on the options to subset the patients by. 

Get an overview over the number of entries for each cancer type (`OncotreeLineage`):

```{r}
models[, .N, by = OncotreeLineage]
```

We can combine multiple operations in one step, by connecting the brackets `[][]`. Lets sort the cancer types by their number of observations: 
```{r}
models[, .N, by = OncotreeLineage][order(N, decreasing = TRUE)]
```

### Filtering datatables

Filtering means creating a logical vector and only returning the rows where the vector is `TRUE`. 

| Operator | Description |
|---|---|
| `==` | is equal |
| `!=` | is unequal |
| `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` | larger, smaller, greater or equal, ... |
| `%in%` | required if we filter for more than one entry |

Filtering criteria can be used and combined using `&` to subset the data. This operation returns entries for non-caucasian patients with breast or Lung cancer: 

```{r}
models[PatientRace != "caucasian" & OncotreeLineage %in% c("Breast", "Lung")]
```

Lets combine filtering and column subsetting. This returns only the columns Sex and Age only for female patients: 

```{r}
models[Sex == "Female", .(Sex, Age)]
```

How many entries for `female` patients older than `30` years are in `models`?

```{r}
models[Age > 30 & Sex == "Female", .N]
```


Instead of only counting rows, we can summarize numeric data using aggregation functions instead of only counting rows. `mean()` returns the mean value of a vector: 

```{r}
models[, .(Age = mean(Age))]
```

### NAs

`NAs` ("not available") are missing values. They will occur in your data. Operations involving `NAs` often return `NA`. Therefore, many functions offer something like `na.rm` to ignore them: 

```{r}
sum(c(2, 12, NA))

sum(c(2, 12, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
```

`is.na()` tests if a value is NA. This is useful for filtering entries. 

```{r}
models[, .N, by = is.na(Age)]
```

To get the mean age ignoring NAs, we can either do this: 

```{r}
models[!is.na(Age), .(mean_age = mean(Age))]
```
or this: 
```{r}
models[, .(mean_age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE))]
```


We can create new columns with `by`, too: 

```{r}
models[, .(mean_age = mean(Age), N = .N), by = .(age_is_NA = is.na(Age))]
```


Now its your turn: For patients with `breast` cancer, what is the number of observations and the mean age, for each gender? 

```{r}
models[OncotreeLineage == "Breast", .(n_patients = .N, mean_age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE)), by = Sex]
```


## Handling arrays

Arrays are great for storing large amounts of only-numeric data. In contrast to data.tables, they can have many more than two dimensions. 

Lets explore our expression dataset. How many dimensions does the object have? What do they store?

```{r}
str(expression)
```

We can subset arrays using vectors of numbers or characters: 

```{r}
expression[1:5,10:20]
expression[c("ACH-001339", "ACH-001619", "ACH-001979"),c("STPG1", "CFTR")]
```

A very useful function to know when dealing with arrays is `apply()`. It allows very fast computations of aggregation functions (like `mean`, `sum` or `length`) on the whole array. Lets compute the mean expression for three genes across all columns of the dataset: 

```{r}
apply(expression[,oncogenes], 2, mean)
```

Other useful R functions: 

| Function | Returns / Explanation |
|---|---|
| `?mean()` | help and additional information on the `mean` function |
| `dim()` | dimensions |
| `dimnames()` | dimension names |
| `intersect(a, b)` | elements in a and b |
| `setdiff()` | elements of a that are not in b |
| `cor()` | computes a correlation |

## ggplot

`ggplot` (or `ggplot2`) is one of the most popular systems to create sophisticated plots, and is highly popular in science. Learning `ggplot` prepares you for creating all kinds of data visualizations. 

A ggplot consists of a minimum of three objects: 
1. data (a datatable or data frame with the information to build the plot)
2. mapping: an aesthetics object (`aes()`) defines which information is mapped where in the plot
3. geometries define the layout of the plot. 

Example: 

```{r}

plot_data <- models[, .(n_obs = .N), OncotreeLineage][n_obs > 50]

ggplot(
  data = plot_data, 
  mapping = aes(x = n_obs, y = OncotreeLineage)) + 
  geom_col()

```


Lets explore what happened here. 
First, we compute the number of observations by Lineage and subset the resulting datatable for Lineages with more than 20 entries. 
This is used as input data for ggplot. In `aes()`, n_obs is mapped on the x-axis, the lineage on y. Finally, we add `geom_col()` to our plot, to define a bar plot. 

By adding more objects to the ggplot using `+`, we can start plotting 
```{r}

plot_data <- models[Sex %in% c("Male", "Female"), .(n_obs = .N), by = .(Sex, OncotreeLineage)]

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = n_obs, y = OncotreeLineage, fill = Sex)) + 
    geom_col(color = "black") + 
    labs(x = "# Observations", y = "Tissue type") + 
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Lets try a boxplot to visualize the age ranges for some tumor type: 
```{r}
plot_data <- models[Sex %in% c("Male", "Female") & 
    OncotreeLineage %in% c("Peripheral Nervous System", "Testis", "Kidney", "Bowel")]

ggplot(plot_data, 
aes(Age, OncotreeLineage, color = Sex)) + 
    geom_boxplot() + 
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```


If you want to explore what is possible with ggplot, feel free to explore [https://r-graph-gallery.com/](https://r-graph-gallery.com/).
